content_list.content_text: With the arrival of the new millennium, Latin American cinema emerged as one of the best in the world. A generation of Mexican, Brazilian, Argentine, Chilean, and Peruvian filmmakers made films that captivated audiences in their own countries and around the globe. These directors won numerous awards, and some of them use their international standing to act as ambassadors for their respective national industries. In the early 1990s, such favorable circumstances would have been unimaginable.

information.contentText: The film is considered a classic and one of the most important Brazilian films ever made, as it marked a major milestone in the revival of Brazilian film production known as the "cinema da retomada" (the "Retomada", or rebirth, of Brazilian cinema), and restored confidence in the national cinema. Montenegro's performance was acclaimed by critics and the press in Brazil and abroad and earned her an Oscar nomination for Best Actress — making her the first Latin American woman, the only Brazilian, and also the only actress ever nominated for the award for a Portuguese-language performance — as well as a Golden Globe nomination for Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Drama.

content_list.content_text: In Mexico, years of poorly planned state intervention, along with distribution problems, had stripped the national cinema of its quality and its identity. By the mid-1990s, film production had fallen to the levels of the 1930s. Alfonso Cuarón (b. 1961) and Guillermo del Toro (b. 1964) were just two of the directors who stood out — with Solo con tu pareja (1992) and Cronos (1993) — but who felt that the only way forward was to leave for Hollywood.

quote.quote: Whenever you want to remember me, take a look at the picture we took together. I'm saying this because I'm afraid that one day you'll forget me.
quote.author: Dora (Fernanda Montenegro) in Central Station

content_list.content_text: The problems faced by the South American film industries were inextricably linked to the turbulent recent history of these societies. Dictatorships, institutionalized corruption, and ill-fated neoliberal experiments took their toll on cinema, including censorship, scarce funding, exile, and even murder. Add to this cultural turmoil on the continent the fact that thousands of movie theaters were converted into evangelical churches.

information.contentText: It is the first in a trilogy of films by the director made up of several sub-narratives connected to the same event. The other two films are 21 Grams, from 2003, and Babel, from 2006.

content_list.content_text: A bitter irony for Brazil, Argentina, and Mexico — the traditional powerhouses of Latin American cinema — was that their respective dictatorial governments were followed by democratically elected but philistine presidents who proved just as harmful to the national film industries as their predecessors. During President Fernando Collor de Mello's term, Brazil's film production shrank to a single feature film in three years, and in 1991 director Hector Babenco (b. 1946) declared, "Brazilian cinema is dead." That makes the country's subsequent comeback all the more extraordinary.

content_list.title: The Landmark of Brazilian Cinema
content_list.description:
City of God, released in 2002, changed the way films are made in Brazil, because its language is different from anything that had been done until then. It also changed the way poverty, destitution, the favelas, and crime were portrayed in the country's audiovisual works. The creative freedom given by the people in charge of the project made a big difference in the final result.

It all began with the book Cidade de Deus (City of God), which was the product of extensive research and was intended, according to its author Paulo Lins, a former resident of Cidade de Deus, to reduce violence in the favela, police violence. Published in 1997, the book did not achieve Lins's goal, and he even declared that his work had been in vain. But the success and the mark left by the film prove the writer was wrong.

Bráulio Mantovani (b. 1963) was chosen by Fernando Meirelles for the task of turning the book into a screenplay. "By page 100 I thought it was impossible." Difficulties aside, the screenplay was written and the film was made by Meirelles and Kátia Lund (b. 1966), with lush cinematography by César Charlone (b. 1958). Upon release, it took a beating from the Brazilian film press. However, audiences and the Hollywood Academy saw it differently. Besides its success in theaters, in 2004 the film received four Oscar nominations: Mantovani competed for Best Adapted Screenplay; Charlone for Best Cinematography; Daniel Rezende, the editor, for Best Film Editing; and Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund were nominated for Best Director.

Brazil caught the world's attention a few years after Central Station had won the Golden Lion at the Berlin Film Festival, showing that it had not been luck and that the country was entering a new era of great works. Several subsequent films followed this school, such as Elite Squad (2007) and Carandiru (2003).
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Meteoro por Trás da Cena: como Cidade de Deus mudou o cinema brasileiro" ("Meteor Behind the Scenes: How City of God Changed Brazilian Cinema"), on uol.com.

content_list.content_text: In South America, this renaissance coincides with the beginning of a process of strengthening political democracy and economies across the continent. Brazil and Argentina were the first to introduce new film laws: the Brazilian government offered tax incentives in exchange for private-sector investment in national films, while Argentina rebuilt its dilapidated system of state subsidies. Other countries gradually followed these examples.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Y Tu Mamá También
information.contentText: The film's explicit depiction of sex and drug use caused complications with its rating. Nevertheless, in Mexico the film grossed US$2.2 million in its opening weekend in June 2001, a record for Mexican cinema at the time.

content_list.content_text: The first signs of recovery came in 1998, when Central Station (1998), by Walter Salles (b. 1956), won the Golden Lion at the Berlin Film Festival. Salles's film was soon followed by two Mexican productions, Amores perros (2000), by Alejandro González Iñárritu (b. 1963), and Cuarón's Y tu mamá también (2001), as well as by City of God (2002), by Brazilian Fernando Meirelles (b. 1955). This quartet of films announced to the world the strong moment these film industries were enjoying.

Behind this promising moment lay a series of specific waves or movements: the Retomada (the rebirth of Brazilian cinema), New Mexican Cinema, New Argentine Cinema, and New Chilean Cinema. In Brazil there is a palpable sense of a filmmaking community, partly thanks to the influence of director-producers Salles and Meirelles, who encourage new filmmakers through their production companies — respectively, Rio de Janeiro-based VideoFilmes and São Paulo's O2 Filmes.

information.contentText: City of God is considered one of the most important Brazilian films of all time, praised by critics, who generally emphasized its artistic and aesthetic qualities. The feature marks the final milestone of the revival of Brazilian film production known as the "cinema da retomada", and it shifted the paradigm of Brazilian cinema by being the only one so far to receive four Oscar nominations, for Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Film Editing, and Best Cinematography.

content_list.content_text: An essential theme of these films is the search for meaning and personal fulfillment, as can be seen in Love for Sale (2006), a poetic film by Karim Ainouz (b. 1966) centered on a single mother's desire for self-determination; in the unsettling Happy Desert (2007), by Paulo Caldas (b. 1964), about a girl's entry into the world of prostitution and her attempt to escape it; and in Antônia (2007), by Tata Amaral (b. 1961), about a São Paulo music group and its struggle to get out of the favela through a record deal.

quote.quote: The film is undeniably the work of an artist with the strength to look into the abyss, resulting in a strengthened humanity.
quote.author: Stephen Holden on Carandiru

content_list.content_text: The themes of brilliant and provocative independent filmmaker Beto Brant (b. 1964) range from the criminal underworld of O Invasor (2002), through the rich mix of art, physical disability, and sexual obsession in Delicate Crime (2005), to the tragic love story of Stray Dog (2007).

information.contentText: Actor Doug Jones, who played the Faun and the "Pale Man," had worked with del Toro on Mimic and Hellboy, and said the director sent him an email that read: "You have to be in this film. No one else can play this part but you." Jones enthusiastically replied after reading an English version of the screenplay, but later discovered that the film was in Spanish, a language he did not speak. He said he was "terrified" and that del Toro suggested learning the screenplay phonetically, which Jones turned down, preferring to learn the words on his own.

content_list.content_text: The Mexicans, whose success is due to the efforts of producers and backers rather than to a healthy industrial infrastructure, displayed the most effervescent facet of this new wave. Amores Perros is an electrifying, structurally ambitious, visceral, and disconcerting film that launched the international careers of González Iñárritu, screenwriter Guillermo Arriaga (b. 1958), and star Gael García Bernal (b. 1978). Together with Diego Luna (b. 1979), Bernal also starred in Y Tu Mamá También, whose director had returned to Mexico after making two films in Hollywood and produced a picture that is at once a road movie, a coming-of-age story, and a portrait of his country, all combined into one sensual blend.

The rigorous, artful combination of sex, faith, and meticulous aesthetics in Japón (2003), Batalla en el cielo (Battle in Heaven, 2005), and Stellet Licht (Silent Light, 2007), by Carlos Reygadas (b. 1971), drew both praise and controversy. Temporada de patos (Duck Season, 2004), by Fernando Eimbcke (b. 1970), was a glorious and hugely popular comedy about adolescence. Del Toro split his time between American projects and Spanish-Mexican co-productions, his mastery of fantasy allowing him to create both the escapism of Hellboy (2004) and the frightening, profound El laberinto del fauno (Pan's Labyrinth, 2006). Sin nombre (2009), by Cary Fukunaga (b. 1977), a moving story about gang culture and illegal immigrants, won two awards at the Sundance Film Festival.

information.contentText: It is the first fiction feature by director José Padilha, who had previously directed the documentary Bus 174 (2002). It caused a great stir even before its release, as it was the first Brazilian film to leak onto the pirate market and the internet months before reaching theaters. One of the film's leads, actor Caio Junqueira, went so far as to say that, although he considered piracy a bad thing, he knew it had been "because of it that the work reached the television audience." A survey by Ibope estimated that more than 11 million Brazilians had watched the film illegally – this, however, did not stop the film from succeeding at the box office, opening in first place.

content_list.content_text: The countries of the continent share many political and social experiences, but their film output is understandably diverse. In Argentina, the region's largest source of world-class filmmakers, this variety is extraordinary. Pablo Trapero (b. 1971) epitomizes the talented generation that emerged from the country's newly founded state and private film schools. His realist style, which relies on non-professional actors and real-life subjects, has proved extremely versatile, ranging from his debut, Mundo grúa (1999), a bittersweet story of a middle-aged man trying to rebuild his life, through the road movie Familia rodante (Rolling Family, 2004), to the prison drama Leonera (Lion's Den, 2008).

content_list.title: Between Fantasy and Coldness
content_list.description:
Pan's Labyrinth may well be a grand summary of Mexican director Guillermo del Toro's career. He had worked on effects-heavy projects such as Hellboy (2004), and on others that build an atmosphere of suspense and tension while dealing with otherworldly matters, such as El espinazo del diablo (The Devil's Backbone, 2001). Pan's Labyrinth may be his most mature film. In it, the director manages to bring together his two particular strands. The result is a film that is at once dark and packed with effects.

The film is set in 1944 and tells the story of Ofelia, a young girl who discovers a fantastic world of woodland creatures when her mother takes her to northern Spain to live with her stepfather, a bitter man and brutal officer in General Franco's fascist army. For this production, Del Toro assembles a roster of top-tier Spanish actors that includes Sergi López, Ariadna Gil, Maribel Verdú, and Ivana Baquero, who plays the girl who escapes her savage stepfather by entering a fantasy world.

Set against the backdrop of the period following the Spanish Civil War, the film's striking beauty and the strength of its performances offer the viewer many remarkable moments. "Pan's Labyrinth was a very difficult film," Del Toro told Sight & Sound magazine, "but it also became a battle over my commitment. I gave up my entire salary in order to make the film my way." If the story fails to fully merge reality and fantasy — Pan's Labyrinth consists of two separate halves rather than one spectacular whole — in the end, this does not make Del Toro's achievement any less extraordinary.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Andy Willis, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Carlos Sorín (b. 1944) and Lisandro Alonso (b. 1975) also use amateur actors, the former in tender comedies about poor, provincial Argentines driven by their dreams — Bombón el perro (Bombón: The Dog, 2004) — and the latter drawing on a minimalist style to explore the isolation and alienation of those on the margins of society, in films such as La libertad (2001) and Los muertos (2004). By contrast, Daniel Burman (b. 1973) created wry explorations of Jewish identity and father-son relationships — Esperando al Mesías (Waiting for the Messiah, 2000), El abrazo partido (Lost Embrace, 2004), and Derecho de familia (Family Law, 2006) — that earned him the nickname "the Woody Allen of Buenos Aires." Meanwhile, the refined, sensory style of Lucrecia Martel (b. 1966) in La Ciénaga (2001), La niña santa (The Holy Girl, 2004), and La mujer sin cabeza (The Headless Woman, 2008) offers scathing views of the family, sexuality, and the stagnant bourgeoisie of her country.

information.contentText: Larraín's film was selected as Chile's submission for the 2009 Oscars.

content_list.content_text: Machuca (2004), by Chilean director Andrés Wood (b. 1965), focuses on the events that would lead to Pinochet's coup. Resisting the national tendency to favor international productions, it inspired a younger generation of filmmakers to be more original — while always keeping an eye on foreign festivals and markets. Many of these new directors examine the country's current situation, notably Alicia Scherson (b. 1974), with the enigmatic Play (2005), and Sebastián Silva (b. 1979), with the complex black comedy La nana (The Maid, 2009). In the deliciously perverse Tony Manero (2008) and Post Mortem (2010), Pablo Larraín (b. 1976) offers chilling glimpses of life under the dictatorship.

One of the most popular films of this era is the melancholy Uruguayan comedy Whisky (2004), by Juan Pablo Rebella (1974-2006) and Pablo Stoll (b. 1974). Peru's Claudia Llosa (b. 1976) deservedly won the Golden Lion at the Berlin Film Festival for The Milk of Sorrow, a local film about the clash between urban life and rural superstition.

quote.quote: Iñárritu's style contains elements of Tarantino, Peckinpah, and others, but ultimately the synthesis is all his own.
quote.author: James Berardinelli on Amores Perros

content_list.content_text: The common denominator that unites all these directors is not their style but their attitude. With no interest in making genre films or aping Hollywood, they make personal films, true to their own experiences, concerns, and cinematic language. The school that has exerted the greatest influence on the continent is probably Neorealism. Although they are not polemical, these Latin American films shed light on the political, social, and even psychological problems of their countries, reflecting on what it means to be Latin American after years of struggle.

information.contentText: The film was shot in Torreón, Coahuila, and in Mexico. Several of the extras used in the film were real migrants. Fukunaga said of working with them: "I didn't have to tell them anything — they know how to sit on top of a train."

content_list.content_text: Although their stories are ostensibly regional, they are told with a flair that makes them universal. This Latin American renaissance is marked by a surprisingly large number of women filmmakers, a thriving documentary scene, and a spirit of collaboration both at home and abroad.

Although the Mexican government was slow to step in (it increased the state budget devoted to film only in 2004), there is a bubbling entrepreneurial spirit among the country's filmmakers — González Iñárritu, Cuarón, and Del Toro joined forces to found the production company Cha Cha Cha, while actors Bernal and Luna and producer Pablo Cruz did the same with their Canana. Similarly, Salles and Meirelles successfully balance international careers with productions in their own country.

information.contentText: The film was selected as Colombia's submission for the 2010 Oscars, presented by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

content_list.content_text: In 2003, the Colombian government introduced laws supporting national cinema and a film fund to boost Colombian production. The result was an increase in the number of films made and a greater international presence. Two notable films, both released in 2009, are El vuelco del cangrejo (Crab Trap, 2009), by Oscar Ruiz Navia (b. 1982), an engaging, beautifully shot conflict between tradition and modernity set in a coastal village in Colombia, and Los viajes del viento (The Wind Journeys, 2009), by Ciro Guerra (b. 1981), an original fable about a legendary accordion player, with performance sequences that are at once cinematic and a musical tour de force.

content_list.title: Iñárritu's Brutality
content_list.description:
Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963) had such a strong and immediate effect on American filmmakers that it was only a matter of time before his influence spread to other countries. Amores Perros proves that by 2000 the Tarantino model of stylized violence and interwoven narratives had already made it south of the American border, to Mexico. The film marks the feature debut of Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu and, although the film ultimately offers nothing particularly new, his vibrant direction manages to inject energy, humor, intelligence, and tenderness into familiar plots.

Shot as three intertwined stories whose central characters meet at a certain key moment, Amores Perros stays true to the "canine" theme of its original title (Amores perros, in Spanish), as each segment of the film gives dogs a prominent role. In the first, a young man has an affair with his brother's wife and enters his prize dog in gruesome (and viscerally effective) fights in the hope of winning money to run away with his sister-in-law. In the second, a plot worthy of Edgar Allan Poe seen through the eyes of Luis Buñuel, a vain, crippled model loses her dog in a space beneath the floor of her apartment and is tormented by the sounds of the animal's incessant suffering, as well as by her inability to resolve the situation. In the last, a homeless hit man seeks redemption for the life he has led and recognition from his family, from whom he has long been estranged.

All three segments ironically illustrate man's inhumanity to his fellow man through his treatment of animals, which in turn suffer so much in the film that Amores Perros displays a conspicuous notice that no animals were mistreated during the making of the film. In fact, the frequent violence of the dogs (and violence against the dogs) is portrayed so realistically that it sometimes threatens to overwhelm the film. But Iñárritu manages to convey his message of bloody betrayal, callous dishonesty, and class division with an abundance of style, revealing in the process a powerful confidence in his actors' instincts as well as in his audience's intelligence.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: In Venezuela, President Hugo Chávez seeks to take on "the dictatorship of Hollywood" with a new state-run studio, Villa del Cine, for the production of national feature films and documentaries. There are grants for independent filmmakers and exhibition laws to ensure that every Venezuelan film produced reaches the screen.

information.contentText: Carandiru tells some of the stories of the inmates of the penitentiary, which was the largest prison in Latin America; the film's story culminates in the 1992 massacre that took place there, in which 111 prisoners were killed, 102 of them by the police. The prison itself was used to shoot some scenes before it was demolished in 2002, a year before the film's release.

content_list.content_text: A peaceful revolution is already sweeping Latin America — not political but cultural — one that promises to topple Hollywood's grip on movie theaters and popularize Latin American films with their domestic audiences. While this struggle continues, the best of these filmmakers are telling their stories in their own way and discovering that the rest of the world is watching.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Demetrios Matheou, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: City of God
movies.overview: Buscapé was raised in a very violent environment. Despite the feeling that all odds were against him, he finds out that life can be seen with other eyes...

movies.title: Amores Perros
movies.overview: A fatalistic car crash in Mexico City sets off a chain of events in the lives of three persons: a young man aching to run off with his sister-in-law, a supermodel, and a homeless man. Their lives are catapulted into unforeseen circumstances instigated by the seemingly inconsequential destiny of a dog.

movies.title: Y Tu Mamá También
movies.overview: In Mexico, two teenage boys and an attractive older woman embark on a road trip and learn a thing or two about life, friendship, sex, and each other.

movies.title: Pan's Labyrinth
movies.overview: Living with her tyrannical stepfather in a new home with her pregnant mother, 10-year-old Ofelia feels alone until she explores a decaying labyrinth guarded by a mysterious faun who claims to know her destiny. If she wishes to return to her real father, Ofelia must complete three terrifying tasks.

movies.title: Central Station
movies.overview: An emotive journey of a former school teacher, who writes letters for illiterate people, and a young boy, whose mother has just died, as they search for the father he never knew.

movies.title: Battle in Heaven
movies.overview: Set in Mexico City, Carlos Reygadas's sexually explicit drama centers on a man in turmoil over his past actions. Chauffer Marcos feels compelled to reveal a dark secret to his boss's daughter, Ana, a wealthy woman who works as a prostitute just for the thrill of it. Marcos confesses that he and his wife committed a crime that ended in horrible tragedy. Haunted by his past, Marcos searches for redemption.

movies.title: Tony Manero
movies.overview: A man is obsessed with John Travolta's disco dancing character from "Saturday Night Fever".

movies.title: Sin Nombre
movies.overview: Sayra, a Honduran teen, hungers for a better life. Her chance for one comes when she is reunited with her long-estranged father, who intends to emigrate to Mexico and then enter the United States. Sayra's life collides with a pair of Mexican gangmembers who have boarded the same American-bound train.

movies.title: Elite Squad
movies.overview: In 1997, before the visit of the pope to Rio de Janeiro, Captain Nascimento from BOPE (Special Police Operations Battalion) is assigned to eliminate the risks of the drug dealers in a dangerous slum nearby where the pope intends to be lodged.

movies.title: Lion's Den
movies.overview: Julia, a 25 year-old university student, two weeks pregnant, with no criminal record, is sent to prison. Julia murdered the father of her child. This story addresses maternity, jail and Justice; confinement, guilt and solitude; but above all it deals with Julia and her son, Tomas, born inside an Argentinean prison.

movies.title: The Motorcycle Diaries
movies.overview: Based on the journals of Che Guevara, leader of the Cuban Revolution. In his memoirs, Guevara recounts adventures he and best friend Alberto Granado had while crossing South America by motorcycle in the early 1950s.

movies.title: Rolling Family
movies.overview: A wedding invite from an estranged sibiling inspires a grandmother to assemble her family and embark on a roadtrip in a broken down caravan.

movies.title: Family Law
movies.overview: A man in his thirties does not want to be like his father, but that seems to be unavoidable.

movies.title: La Libertad
movies.overview: A woodcutter goes about his work.

movies.title: Whisky
movies.overview: When his long-lost brother resurfaces, Jacobo, desperate to prove his life has added up to something, looks to scrounge up a wife. He turns to Marta, an employee at his sock factory, with whom he has a prickly relationship.

movies.title: The Wind Journeys
movies.overview: After his wife's death, a vallenato singer from Majagual, Sucre, decides to quit music and return his allegedly cursed accordion to his master. He is joined by Fermín Morales, a teenage boy who admires him and wishes to follow his footsteps. Together, they start a journey throughout several towns in Northern Colombia to Taroa, in La Guajira desert, where the singer's master supposedly lives.

movies.title: Carandiru
movies.overview: When a doctor decides to carry out an AIDS prevention program inside Latin America’s largest prison: the Casa de Detenção de São Paulo - Carandiru, he discovers the victim of one of the darkest days in Brazilian History when the State of São Paulo’s Military Police, with the excuse for law enforcement, shot to death 111 people. Based on real facts and on the book written by Dráuzio Varella.

content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1990 to 2009
content_list.description: '90s independent cinema dominates the screens, and animation breaks new ground with Pixar. CGI reaches a new level with The Matrix, and Latin American and European cinemas capture the world's attention. Click here to see a chronological view of the main events in cinema from 1990 to 2009.
